segments.t: College English Test, Band 4, Part 2, Listening Comprehension, Section A, Directions.
In this section, you will hear three news reports.
At the end of each news report, you will hear two or three questions.
Both the news report and the questions will be spoken only once.
After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked A,
B, C, and D. Then mark the corresponding letter on answer sheet one, with a single line through
the center. News report one. A 104-year-old woman is selling the house she has lived in since she was
two years old. Nancy Gifford was born months after the end of the First World War, and spent 102
years living in her three-bedroom house in the Somerset village of St. She is now putting it
on the market, having lived in it through the Second World War and the invention of television.
Her family bought the house for £200 in 1921, and it is now priced at some £170,000.
According to the Bank of England inflation calculator, £200 in 1921 would be worth £7,750 today.
According to the estate agent, the house was built in 1882 and originally featured a
well for the entire road, except for some changes in the toilet and wash area, much of the house
remains the same. Mrs Gifford is selling the house and moving to a nursing home in nearby glass
because of her health. Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
Question 1. What does the news report say about Nancy Gifford? Question 2. Why is Mrs Gifford selling
the house? News report 2. The Navy rescued a man who survived 24 days floating in the sea on a boat
by eating tomato sauce and vegetable powder. The man, 47, wrote the word help in English on the boat,
which was key to his rescue. The man told authorities that his experience began in December,
when currents swept the sailboat out to sea while he was making repairs. To survive, the man collected
rainwater with a cloth. He had to constantly remove water from the boat to prevent it from sinking.
He also tried to light a fire to send a distress signal without success. Finally,
a plane passed by and he signaled with a mirror. He said the Navy told him that he was spotted
when the plane passed again. The sailboat was abandoned at sea when the man was picked up by a nearby
merchant ship. He was found in good health but had lost weight. Questions 3 and 4 are based on
news reports you have just heard. Question 3. What does the news reports say was key to the man's rescue?
Question 4. What do we learn about the man when he was rescued? News report 3. The board of Denver
Public Schools is set to close several elementary and middle schools to make up for a decreased
budget caused by declining enrollment. The specific schools will be announced in the coming days
at district spokesperson said. The school board approved criteria to close schools with fewer than
215 students as well as schools with fewer than 275 students and a projected decline in enrollment.
In the next three years, the district expects to enroll 3,000 fewer elementary and middle school
students it said. 3,000 students may not seem like that many students but to a budget where you're
receiving per pupil funding that's about 36 million dollars. District spokesperson Scott Pribble said.
We know that there are impacts and it's heartbreaking and difficult work but in order for the
district to stay out of debt it's a step that needs to be taken he said. The district said that
the increased budget means it cannot provide the same mental health support, social and emotional
services or specialised programming to schools with lower enrollment. Questions 5 to 7 are based
on the news report you have just heard. Question 5. What do we learn about the elementary and middle
schools to be closed in Denver? Question 6. What does the Denver district expect to do in the next
three years? Question 7. Why are some schools in Denver to be closed according to the district
spokesperson? Section B. Directions. In this section you will hear two long conversations.
At the end of each conversation you will hear four questions. Both the conversation and the
questions will be spoken only once. After you hear a question you must choose the best answer
from the four choices marked A, B, C and D. Then mark the corresponding letter on answer sheet 1
with a single line through the center. Conversation 1. Good afternoon. Theatre Bookings International.
My name is Philip. How may I help you today? Oh good afternoon. My name is Helen. I've been trying
to book tickets for the musical cats in London on the evening of May the 28th. But I
can't get the computer to accept my card payment. I've tried three times, but it just doesn't want
to take it. That's okay, Madam. I can book it and take the payment over the phone if that's not
a problem for you. That would be wonderful. I'm not very good with computers. My husband usually
does all of these things, but he isn't Italy on a business trip until next Thursday. And I know
how quickly these things can sell out. They do indeed, Madam. Firstly, can you confirm that it's the
performance of Cats on May the 28th at the Lion Theatre in London at 7.30 p.m.? Yes, that's the one.
And I will need two tickets, please. Not too close to the front. Actually, all the tickets at the
front are already sold out anyway. But I can offer you two upstairs near the middle. I assume that
you don't want to be too high up. Oh my goodness. No, I'm scared of heights. And you can never see
anything if you are too high up anyway. No problem, Madam. I'll reserve those for you now.
And all we need after that is the details of your card number and your full name. And then we are done.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
Question 8. Why does the woman call the man? Question 9. What do we learn about the woman's husband?
Question 10. What does the man say about the tickets at the front? Question 11. What does the woman say
she is scared of? Conversation 2. Hi, John. Why haven't you answered my text messages lately?
Oh, I didn't know you had sent any. I turned off my phone almost a week ago and haven't
turned it back on since then. Why would you do something like that? When our phones make our
lives so much more convenient? Well, I downloaded an app that recorded how much time I spent on my phone
and I was shocked to realize I was using my phone an average of eight hours a day. And on my worst
day, I used it for 12 hours. Were you addicted to mobile phone games? I had a friend who was
and he sometimes played them all day and into the night. No, my problem was I was spending
too much time on social media, messaging friends and commenting on other people's posts.
I do all of that too, as well as shopping online and paying for everything with my phone.
That is really why I don't see how anyone could live without a mobile phone. How do you buy things
or communicate with your friends? Since I stopped using my phone, I go to physical stores and
pay in cash. I've actually met friends for meals at cafes and restaurants.
That's great for you, but my friends and family don't live in this city. So we can't see each
other often and I don't have any choice but to chat with them online. Questions 12 to 15 are based
on the conversation you have just heard. Question 12. Why hasn't the man answered the woman's text messages
lately? Question 13. What was the man shocked to realise after he downloaded the app?
Question 14. What did the man spend much time doing with his phone? Question 15. Why does the woman
say she has to use her mobile phone? Section C. Directions. In this section you will hear three
passages. At the end of each passage you will hear three or four questions. Both the passage
and the questions will be spoken only once. After you hear a question you must choose the best answer
from the four choices marked A, B, C and D. Then mark the corresponding letter on answer sheet
1 with a single line through the centre. Passage 1. If US workers want to switch jobs,
they'd better do it now. Last year, job switchers earned far higher wage increases than those
staying in their jobs, but the gap is now closing. A three month moving average of annual wage increases
from the Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank's wage tracker shows that US job switchers got the highest
wage increase last July, when the measure touched 8.5%. Since then it has gone up and down
and has been going steadily down since November. The gap in wage gains between people who switched
jobs and those who stayed in their jobs is now closing. On average, people who changed jobs
have almost always gotten better pay raises than those who stayed. But in the past, the difference
was usually around 1 percentage point. In July though, the gap widened to 2.6 percentage points.
But now wage growth is slowing down for everyone, and job switchers are getting smaller wage
bumps in their new jobs. At the moment, those who change jobs get an average 7.3% raise every year,
while those who stay get a 5.4% raise. That suggests the demand for workers has reached,
or is at least nearing its peak. The labor market is likely cooling because even a shortage of workers
isn't overcoming the historic imbalance between employers and employees in the US.
The volume of income that workers take home as a proportion of what the US economy produces
is still falling. Question 16-18 are based on the passage you have just heard.
Question 16. What does the passage say about the gap in wage gains between job switchers and
those who stay in their jobs? Question 17. What do we learn about wage growth now? Question 18.
What is the labor market likely doing according to the passage?
Passage 2. Highly processed foods, the kinds made with lots of sugar, fat and salt,
make up as much as 60% of the average American diet. But a new study shows that their low price
and convenience come at a cost to health. The study found that, when people ate a highly processed
diet, they consumed about 500 more calories per day than they did when they ate a less processed
diet. They also gained 2 pounds over 2 weeks, even though both diets had the same amounts of
nutrients, like sugar, fat, fiber and salt. It wasn't a shock to find highly processed foods
weren't healthy. Other research has linked them to a higher risk of cancer and obesity.
What was unexpected was that sugar, fat and salt didn't seem to be what caused people
to overeat. This is the first trial that demonstrates that there is something about highly processed
foods, independence of those nutrients that causes people to overeat. The study also found that,
when eating a highly processed diet, people ate faster. This could be one reason why they gained
more weight. Highly processed food tends to be softer, which makes it easier to chew and swallow.
One theory is that if you're eating more quickly, you're not giving your gut enough time to
signal to your brain that you've had enough calories and let your full. By the time the brain gets
that signal, you've already overeat. Questions 19-21 are based on the passage you have just heard.
Question 19- What does a new study show about highly processed foods? Question 20- What are
highly processed foods linked to, according to other research? Question 21- What do people tend to do
when eating highly processed foods? Passage 3- Women continue to spend more time than men
taking care of children and doing chores around the house. This is generally attributed to backward
thinking and conservative values, but new research shows that such differences could be linked to
differences in the preferences of males and females. The new study looked at how men and women
were dividing work at home and why they divided it that way. In general, both men and women took
more responsibility for tasks they liked. For example, men liked yard care and home maintenance
more than women. They leaned toward wanting primary responsibility for such tasks.
The researchers stated that differences in enjoyment of household and child care tasks matched
how men and women chose to split tasks. The researchers added that there was not a single
child care task that men liked more than women. Keep in mind, however, that as with any research
on group differences, there were large within group differences. The study's authors concluded
that differences in men's and women's time spent on child care and household tasks do not mean
dissatisfaction. The authors noted that previous research revealed gender differences in attitudes
towards family and career. These differences appear as early as six years old. Girls that age
already show more interest in helping and caring for others than boys do, and they already exhibit
a greater orientation toward family versus career. Questions 22 to 25 are based on the
passage you have just heard. Question 22. How do people generally account for differences between
men and women in the amount of time spent on housework? Question 23. What did men lean toward
doing according to the new study? Question 24. What should we keep in mind as regards any research
on group differences? Question 25. What did previous research reveal about gender differences
in attitudes toward family and career? That's the end of listening comprehension.
